sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Chapter 7 discusses the factors that promote or inhibit corrosion of soil nails, criteria for assessing soil corrosion potential, and guidelines for selecting levels of corrosion protection. Permanent walls need thorough consideration of the corrosion potential of tendons and other metallic components. The grouted tendons always have some protection, but grout alone cannot protect them in aggressive ground. The chapter covers solid bar soil nails; HBSNs, whose options are more limited, are in Chapter 10.
sections.body: 7.1 Introduction (p. 205). This chapter discusses the main factors that promote or inhibit corrosion in soil nails, presents criteria for assessing soil corrosion potential, and introduces guidelines for selecting levels of corrosion protection. The design and construction of permanent soil nail walls require a thorough consideration of the corrosion potential of tendons and other metallic components. The tendons discussed in the manual are grouted, so some level of corrosion protection always exists; however, grout alone cannot provide adequate corrosion protection for aggressive ground conditions. The chapter focuses on corrosion protection for solid bar soil nails; HBSNs are discussed in Chapter 10, and their protection options are limited compared with solid bars because of the methods used to install them.
key_points: Grouted soil nails always have some corrosion protection
Grout alone cannot provide adequate protection in aggressive ground
Permanent walls need thorough consideration of the corrosion potential of tendons and other metallic components
Chapter 7 covers solid bar soil nails; HBSNs are in Chapter 10, with more limited options
sections.applicability: Corrosion protection of permanent solid bar soil nail walls.

sections.title: Historical Background
sections.summary: No published reports describe soil nail wall failures or serviceability problems from tendon corrosion, so the manual's recommendations come from other earth retention systems: ground anchors (Weatherby 1982; PTI 2004, whose decision tree selects protection levels; Sabatini et al. 1999; AASHTO 2014 and AASHTO 2002 Section 6) and MSE wall reinforcement. Corrosion protection classes, criteria separating strong and mild corrosion potential, and a decision tree are adapted to soil nails.
sections.body: 7.2 Historical Background (pp. 205-206). There are no publications reporting soil nail wall failures or serviceability issues due to corrosion of the tendons, so the recommendations follow from experience with other earth retention systems; publications on corrosion of ground anchors and of MSE wall metallic reinforcement provide relevant information. Ground anchor references: Tiebacks (Weatherby 1982), which discusses corrosion effects on prestressed anchors and the mostly European practice of the time; PTI (2004) Recommendations for Prestressed Rock and Soil Anchors, with a decision tree for selecting protection levels based on soil aggressiveness and risk assessment including cost; Ground Anchors (Sabatini et al. 1999), with a similar decision tree; and AASHTO (2014) and AASHTO (2002) Section 6 Ground Anchors. Although specific to prestressed anchors, certain aspects extend to soil nails: the concept of corrosion protection classes, criteria differentiating strong and mild corrosion potential, and increasing protection levels selected with a decision tree similar to PTI (2004) and Sabatini et al. (1999).
key_points: No published soil nail wall failures or serviceability issues from tendon corrosion
Recommendations adapted from ground anchor and MSE wall experience
Ground anchor references: Weatherby (1982), PTI (2004), Sabatini et al. (1999), AASHTO (2014), AASHTO (2002) Section 6
PTI (2004) and Sabatini et al. (1999) decision trees for selecting protection levels
Adapted to soil nails: protection classes, strong/mild corrosion potential criteria, decision tree
sections.applicability: Background to the soil nail corrosion protection framework and its sources.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.summary: Terms used in the chapter: aggressiveness (tendency of soil to corrode steel at relatively fast rates); aggressive and non-aggressive soil (resistivity, pH, sulfate and chloride above or within the thresholds of Elias et al. 2009); corrosion potential (similar to aggressiveness); Class A protection (encapsulation in plastic sheathing), Class B (epoxy coating or galvanizing of tendon and connection components), Class C (bare tendon, grout only); passivation. The classes differ from previous editions of the manual.
sections.body: 7.3 Terminology (p. 206). Aggressiveness: the tendency of the soil to promote corrosion of steel at relatively fast rates. Aggressive soil: a soil with values of resistivity, pH, sulfate and chloride contents that exceed established thresholds (Elias et al. 2009) and that promote corrosion of steel at relatively fast rates. Non-aggressive soil: values that do not exceed those thresholds. Corrosion potential: similar to aggressiveness. Class A protection: encapsulation of the soil nail in plastic sheathing. Class B protection: epoxy coating or galvanizing the tendon and connection components. Class C protection: a bare tendon with no protective coatings other than the surrounding grout. Passivation: the process by which a metal corrodes and forms an outer layer of corrosion, causing it to become less reactive and more passive. The process for selecting the corrosion protection type, and the characteristics of Classes A, B and C, are different from those in previous versions of the manual.
key_points: Aggressive soil: resistivity, pH, sulfate and chloride exceed thresholds (Elias et al. 2009)
Corrosion potential is similar to aggressiveness
Class A: encapsulation in plastic sheathing
Class B: epoxy coating or galvanizing of the tendon and connection components
Class C: bare tendon with no coating other than the grout
Classes A-C and their selection differ from previous editions
sections.applicability: Terms used for corrosion potential and protection classes of soil nails.

sections.title: Corrosion Mechanisms
sections.summary: Corrosion is the electrochemical deterioration of a metal by ion movement from an anode to a cathode through an electrolyte, driven by differences in voltage, oxygen, pH or resistivity. Of seven types, general corrosion, localized corrosion (pitting) and stray-current corrosion matter most for soil nails; stress crack corrosion and hydrogen embrittlement occur typically in prestressing steel. Intact grout protects by barrier and passivation (pH > 13); cracks reaching the tendon promote pitting. Stray current risk is very small beyond about 100 to 200 ft.
sections.body:
7.4.1 Overview (p. 207). Corrosion deteriorates a refined metal by changing its physical and chemical properties and may ultimately dissolve it through electrochemical reactions: movement of ions from a metal surface (anode) to another (cathode) through an electrolyte such as dissolved oxygen, chlorine and hydrogen ions, arising from differences in voltage, oxygen concentration, pH or electric resistivity. For grouted nails, ions can flow between two points along the tendon (Figure 7.1) or between a nearby metallic object and the nail. 7.4.2 Types (pp. 207-208): general, localized, stray-current, stress crack/hydrogen embrittlement, fatigue, bacterial attack and galvanic corrosion (Withiam et al. 1992; Sabatini et al. 1999). The first three are the most significant for soil nails. Stress crack corrosion and hydrogen embrittlement occur typically in prestressing bars and strands for ground anchors, where tensile stresses are much higher than in soil nails; fatigue corrosion needs pronounced cyclic loading; bacterial attack occurs where bacteria reduce sulfate under anaerobic conditions; galvanic corrosion is not seen with appropriate materials.
7.4.2a General Corrosion (p. 208): a uniformly distributed, thin layer of rust that may develop when steel is left unprotected on site, handled improperly or stored inadequately; once the very small passive film forms, the oxidation rate decreases and the rust layer is often favorable. Without inhibiting conditions, general corrosion may be significant over the typical design life of at least 75 years for permanent highway structures. Wax, oil or other temporary coatings should not be used on stockpiled tendons. 7.4.2b Localized Corrosion (p. 209): pitting develops in small pits or crevices. Uncracked grout protects by a physical barrier and chemical passivation (hydroxides from cement hydration give pH > 13 and a protective oxide layer). Cracks through the grout into the tendon promote pitting where oxygen is available; a crack width below 0.004 in. is generally the lower bound cited (Samtani and Nowatzki 2010). Pitting is cause for tendon rejection. 7.4.2c Stray Current (pp. 209-210): prolonged stray currents accelerate corrosion where current leaves the structure; walls with high strength steel (95 to 150 ksi) may be affected; the potential is very small when sources are more than about 100 to 200 ft from the tendons (Elias 2000). A corrosion expert must evaluate projects where stray currents are suspected.
key_points: Electrochemical process: ions move from anode to cathode through an electrolyte
Seven types; general, localized (pitting) and stray-current corrosion are the most significant for soil nails
Stress crack corrosion and hydrogen embrittlement occur typically in prestressing steel for ground anchors
General corrosion: thin uniform rust layer; significant over the 75-year design life only without inhibiting conditions
Intact grout: physical barrier and passivation (pH > 13); cracks into the tendon promote pitting
Crack width below 0.004 in. is the lower bound generally cited (Samtani and Nowatzki 2010)
Stray currents: high strength steel (95-150 ksi) may be affected; risk very small beyond about 100 to 200 ft (Elias 2000)

sections.title: Evaluation of Soil Corrosion Potential
sections.summary: Conditions promoting corrosion: too low or high pH, low resistivity, high chlorides or sulfides, saturated soil, organic content, stray currents and oxygen. Table 7.1 rates resistivity (very corrosive < 700 ohm-cm to non-corrosive > 10,000). Table 7.2 (Elias et al. 2009): ground is aggressive if any threshold is not met (pH 5.0-10, resistivity > 3,000 ohm-cm, sulfates < 200 ppm, chlorides < 100 ppm, organics < 1%); chlorides and sulfates may be waived at resistivity >= 5,000 ohm-cm. Untested ground is assumed aggressive.
sections.body: 7.5.1 Conditions Promoting Corrosion (p. 210): too low or too high pH; low electric resistivity; high concentration of chlorides or sulfides in ground or groundwater; saturated or near-saturated soil; soil with organic content; stray currents; and availability of oxygen. Table 7.1 (NCHRP 1978): very corrosive < 700 ohm-cm; corrosive 700-2,000; moderately corrosive 2,000-5,000; mildly corrosive 5,000-10,000; non-corrosive > 10,000. 7.5.2 Criteria (pp. 211-212): per Table 7.2, based on Elias et al. (2009), the ground is aggressive if any one condition exceeds the listed limit: pH 5.0 < pH < 10 (AASHTO T-289); resistivity greater than 3,000 ohm-cm (AASHTO T-288, which may have limitations for coarse soils with little material finer than the No. 10 sieve); sulfates less than 200 ppm and chlorides less than 100 ppm (ASTM D4327); organics less than 1% by weight (AASHTO T-267). The chloride and sulfate requirements may be waived (printed 'waved') when the resistivity is greater than or equal to 5,000 ohm-cm. Non-aggressive means the corrosion can be tolerated with reasonable confidence within the design life (typically 50 to 75 years) if the electrochemistry does not change. The test method used should be stated. Tests from a nearby site may be used if conditions are similar; if no tests are performed, the ground should be assumed aggressive. Anticipated future changes (road salt, mining, chemical plants or storage) should be considered. For walls supporting roadways exposed to deicing salts, MSE data indicate higher corrosion rates in the upper 8 ft (or deeper with soil gradation); a 30-mil (minimum) geomembrane should be placed below the road base and tied into the roadway drainage, not the wall drainage.
key_points: Conditions promoting corrosion: pH, low resistivity, chlorides/sulfides, saturation, organics, stray currents, oxygen
Table 7.1 resistivity: < 700 very corrosive; 700-2,000; 2,000-5,000; 5,000-10,000; > 10,000 ohm-cm non-corrosive
Aggressive if any Table 7.2 threshold is exceeded
Non-aggressive: 5.0 < pH < 10 (AASHTO T-289); resistivity > 3,000 ohm-cm (AASHTO T-288)
Non-aggressive: sulfates < 200 ppm, chlorides < 100 ppm (ASTM D4327); organics < 1% (AASHTO T-267)
Chloride and sulfate criteria may be waived when resistivity >= 5,000 ohm-cm (Elias et al. 2009)
Without tests, assume aggressive ground
Deicing salts: 30-mil minimum geomembrane below the road base, tied into the roadway drainage

tables.description: Very corrosive < 700 ohm-cm; corrosive 700-2,000; moderately corrosive 2,000-5,000; mildly corrosive 5,000-10,000; non-corrosive > 10,000.

sections.title: Corrosion Protection Systems
sections.summary: Protection is physical, chemical or both (cathodic protection is not typically used). Grout cover is always present, with centralizers giving at least 1 in. of cover, but is not relied on in aggressive ground. Epoxy (ASTM A775 or A934, 7 to 12 mils) and galvanization (at least 2.0 oz/ft2 or 3.4 mils) add protection. Encapsulation uses corrugated PVC (0.04 in.) or HDPE (0.06 in.) sheathing. Sacrificial steel follows Eqs. 7.1-7.2. Nail heads need 2 in. outside and 3 in. soil-side cover; stray currents need electrical isolation.
sections.body: 7.6.1 (pp. 212-213): physical protection places a continuous barrier between the tendon and the corrosion sources; chemical protection uses a sacrificial material (galvanizing) or a dielectric (epoxy, electrical isolation pads); cathodic protection is not typically used. 7.6.2 Grout Cover (p. 213): neat cement grout always covers the tendon; centralizers should give a minimum grout cover of 1 in. between the tendon (bare, epoxy-coated or galvanized) and the soil, allowing for bar sag. Because the grout cracks under tension, most where the critical slip surface crosses the nail, it is conservative not to rely on it in aggressive ground. 7.6.3 Epoxy Coating (pp. 213-215): fusion-bonded epoxy per ASTM A775 or A934, applied by the manufacturer; green (A775, most common, flexible), gray or purple (A934, more chemically resistant; purple suited to marine or harsh environments); no color is favored for longevity. Without site-specific data, protection in aggressive conditions must not rely solely on epoxy. Damage should be repaired when practically possible. Required thickness 7 to 12 mils (ASTM A775 or A934); specify a reasonable range, since excess epoxy can stop couplers and nuts fitting. 7.6.4 Zinc Coating (p. 215): hot-dip galvanizing per AASHTO (2014) or ASTM A123 (A767 as reference); minimum 2.0 oz/ft2 or 3.4 mils (AASHTO 2014 Art. 11.10.6.4.2a); ASTM A123 also requires a 3.4-mil project average and 3.1 mils for an individual tendon; ASTM A153 for nuts, plates and hardware; damage repaired with zinc-rich paint. Grout cover stays 1 in. 7.6.5 Encapsulation (pp. 215-216): common in permanent walls in aggressive or unknown environments; corrugated PVC sheathing of nominal 0.04 in. or HDPE of nominal 0.06 in., the annulus grouted in the shop with at least 0.2 in. internal cover; at least 1 in. of grout outside; couplings by heat shrink over wax tape (PTI 2007); 3-ft sheathings behind the facing have been used (Figure 3.9). 7.6.6 Sacrificial Steel (pp. 216-217): used for MSE reinforcement (Fishman and Withiam 2011); allowed for solid bars by Owner or agency stipulation, but coatings and encapsulation are preferred; X = 80 tf^0.8 (Eq. 7.1), dloss = dbar - 2X (Eq. 7.2). 7.6.7 Nail-Head Protection (p. 217): minimum concrete or shotcrete cover 2 in. outside and 3 in. on the soil side; all head components epoxy coated or galvanized when the tendon is encapsulated, epoxy coated or galvanized, unless the total cover is 9 in. or more in a non-marine environment. 7.6.8 Stray Currents (p. 217): electrical isolation along the path or at the nail (encapsulation can isolate), field-tested after installation and before grouting.
key_points: Grout cover always present; centralizers give at least 1 in. of cover; not relied on in aggressive ground
Epoxy: fusion-bonded, ASTM A775 (green) or A934 (gray, purple), 7 to 12 mils; not relied on alone in aggressive ground
Galvanizing: minimum 2.0 oz/ft2 or 3.4 mils (AASHTO 2014 Art. 11.10.6.4.2a); ASTM A123 3.4-mil average, 3.1-mil individual
Encapsulation: corrugated PVC 0.04 in. or HDPE 0.06 in.; at least 0.2 in. grout inside, 1 in. outside
Sacrificial steel: X (um) = 80 tf^0.8 (Eq. 7.1); dloss = dbar - 2X (Eq. 7.2); coatings and encapsulation preferred
Nail head: cover 2 in. outside and 3 in. soil side; components coated when the tendon is (unless 9 in. cover, non-marine)
Stray currents: electrical isolation, field-tested after installation and before grouting

equations.notes: For plain steel elements (Fishman and Withiam 2011). Units as printed (p. 216).

equations.notes: Steel loss is taken twice from the bar diameter (p. 216); the area with steel loss is used as At in Eq. 6-5 (p. 223).

sections.title: Methodology for Selecting Corrosion Protection Levels
sections.summary: The decision tree of Figure 7.2, adapted from PTI (2004) without its service-life input because only permanent nails are covered, gives the minimum class: aggressive or unknown soil gets Class A (encapsulation); for non-aggressive soil the Owner's risk tolerance decides, low giving Class A, intermediate Class B (epoxy coated or galvanized), high Class C (bare steel, sacrificial steel). Table 7.3 lists the classes. The Owner assesses risk tolerance per project; owners may adopt a higher class.
sections.body: 7.7.1 Introduction (pp. 217-218): factors include perceived consequences of failure, relative cost of protection levels, performance by tendon type, and the effect of installation on some systems; a decision tree and step-by-step procedure account for them. 7.7.2a Overview (pp. 218-219): the methodology for solid bars (Figure 7.2) adapts the PTI (2004) decision tree and deviates from previous FHWA guidance to emphasize the difference between encapsulated and epoxy coated or galvanized bars. The classes are the minimum for permanent soil nails; Owners may adopt a higher class. Service life is omitted from the tree because only permanent elements are addressed. Soil is first classified with Table 7.2: aggressive soils or those with unknown corrosive conditions receive Class A; projects in non-aggressive soils are evaluated for risk tolerance (perceived risks, failure consequences and the added cost of more protection), with uncertainty resolved conservatively. In Figure 7.2: low risk tolerance gives Class A encapsulation, intermediate gives Class B epoxy coated or galvanized, and high gives Class C bare steel (sacrificial steel). Table 7.3: Class A, encapsulation, for aggressive soil or unknown corrosion potential and for non-aggressive soil with low risk tolerance, the highest level used in practice (in extreme situations combined with epoxy or galvanizing); Class B, epoxy coating or galvanization, for non-aggressive soil with intermediate or high risk tolerance (as printed in the table); Class C, bare steel tendon (sacrificial steel), for non-aggressive soil with high risk tolerance; all classes include the grout. 7.7.2b Risk Tolerance (pp. 219-220): assessed by the Owner per project; examples: limited, affordable losses may justify high; costly losses intermediate or low; limited testing with possible injury or loss of life should be low. 7.7.2c (pp. 220-222): Class A (Figure 7.3), Class B (Figure 7.4), Class C (Figure 7.5).
key_points: Figure 7.2 adapts PTI (2004); service life omitted because only permanent nails are covered
Aggressive or unknown soil: Class A (encapsulation)
Non-aggressive soil: low risk tolerance Class A; intermediate Class B (epoxy or galvanized); high Class C (bare/sacrificial steel)
Table 7.3 lists Class B for intermediate or high risk tolerance and Class C for high, as printed
Classes are minimums; Owners may adopt a higher class
Risk tolerance is the Owner's project-specific judgment; possible injury or loss of life calls for low

sections.applicability: Choosing the corrosion protection class (A, B or C) for permanent solid bar soil nails.

sections.title: Design of Corrosion Protection
sections.summary: The Owner selects soil nail corrosion protection in five steps: classify the soil with Table 7.2; pick the protection level from Figure 7.2; select the tendon type; for Class C, compute the sacrificial steel (Eq. 7-1) over the design life (typically 50 to 75 years), the reduced diameter and area, and use that area as At in Eq. 6-5; for Class A or B, complete the design according to Chapter 6.
sections.body: 7.8.1 Design Steps for Corrosion Protection of Soil Nails (pp. 222-223). The selection is performed by the Owner: (1) Use Table 7.2 to classify soil as non-aggressive or aggressive, from corrosion testing per Chapter 4 and this chapter. (2) Use Figure 7.2 to determine the protection level with regard to aggressiveness, risk tolerance and other considerations. (3) Select the appropriate tendon type. (4) If Class C is selected: a. obtain the nominal tendon diameter; b. select the design life (typically 50 to 75 years); c. calculate sacrificial steel using Eq. 7-1; d. calculate the new diameter with steel loss; e. calculate the tendon area with steel loss; f. use that area as At in Eq. 6-5 for the nominal tendon resistance; g. proceed with the design according to Chapter 6. (5) If Class A or B is selected, complete the design according to Chapter 6.
key_points: Step 1: classify the soil with Table 7.2
Step 2: protection level from Figure 7.2
Step 3: select the tendon type
Step 4 (Class C): sacrificial steel by Eq. 7-1 for a 50-75 year design life; reduced area used as At in Eq. 6-5
Step 5 (Class A or B): complete the design per Chapter 6

sections.title: Unusual Conditions
sections.summary: Marine or chloride-rich environments: carbon steel losses of about 3.2 mils per side in the first few years, then 0.67 to 0.7 mils thereafter, and about 3.4 mils of zinc in the first year. Under roads and abutments exposed to de-icing salts, a 30-mil minimum geomembrane below the road base, tied into the roadway drainage. Acidic water from mine waste, abandoned coal mines or pyrite-rich strata may need a corrosion specialist. Such conditions may not suit soil nailing.
sections.body: 7.9 Unusual Conditions (p. 223). Structures exposed to a marine or other chloride-rich environment need further consideration: for marine structures exposed to saltwater, carbon steel losses on the order of 3.2 mils per side or radius should be anticipated in the first few years, reducing to a range from 0.67 to 0.7 mils thereafter. Zinc losses are likely to be quite rapid compared with retained soils meeting the electrochemical criteria; a total zinc loss of approximately 3.4 mils should be anticipated in the first year of exposure. Higher corrosion rates under roads and bridge abutments exposed to de-icing can be addressed by a 30-mil (minimum) geomembrane below the road base tied into the roadway drainage. Structures exposed to acidic water from mine waste, abandoned coal mines or pyrite-rich soil and rock strata may require a corrosion specialist. Such conditions may not be suitable for soil nailing, and the corrosion potential will likely be the strongest factor in the feasibility study.
key_points: Marine: carbon steel loss about 3.2 mils per side in the first few years, then 0.67 to 0.7 mils thereafter
Marine: about 3.4 mils of zinc lost in the first year
De-icing salts: 30-mil minimum geomembrane below the road base tied into the roadway drainage
Acidic mine water or pyrite-rich strata: corrosion specialist; may not suit soil nailing
sections.applicability: Soil nail walls in marine, de-icing salt or acidic ground conditions.
